module_title: Historical Background & Preamble - Supreme Court Judgments, Charter Acts, and Borrowed Features
introduction: This advanced level provides a critical analysis of the centralization process through Charter Acts, the nuances of borrowed features from foreign constitutions, and the deep jurisprudential significance of the Preamble as interpreted by the Supreme Court.

core_concepts.title: Charter Acts (1833 & 1853)
core_concepts.description: 1833 was the final step towards centralization; it made the Governor-General of Bengal the 'Governor-General of India' (Lord William Bentinck). 1853 separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's council.

core_concepts.title: Borrowed Features of the Constitution
core_concepts.description: India borrowed strategically: Fundamental Rights, Judicial Review, and Impeachment from the USA; Directive Principles (DPSP) from Ireland; Parliamentary system and Rule of Law from the UK; Concurrent List and Joint Sitting from Australia.

core_concepts.title: Significance of the Preamble in Law
core_concepts.description: The Preamble indicates the basic structure of the Constitution. However, the Supreme Court has clarified that the Preamble is 'neither a source of power to legislature nor a prohibition upon the powers of legislature'.

core_concepts.title: Criticism of the Constituent Assembly
core_concepts.description: Critics argue it was not a representative body (members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies, not by universal adult franchise) and not a fully sovereign body (created by British proposals), though it acted as one post-independence.

core_concepts.title: Indian Independence Act, 1947
core_concepts.description: It ended British rule, partitioned India, and made the Constituent Assembly a fully sovereign body, empowering it to frame any constitution and abrogate any British law.

important_entities.name: N.A. Palkhivala
important_entities.significance: He famously called the Preamble the 'Identity Card of the Constitution'.

important_entities.name: K.M. Munshi
important_entities.significance: He described the Preamble as the 'Political Horoscope of our Sovereign Democratic Republic'.

important_entities.name: Lord Macaulay
important_entities.significance: Under the Charter Act of 1833, he headed the commission that began codifying Indian laws, leading eventually to the IPC.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Rule of Law vs. Procedure Established by Law
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: UPSC often tests this distinction: 'Rule of Law' is borrowed from the UK Constitution, whereas 'Procedure Established by Law' (Article 21) is borrowed from the Japanese Constitution.

The 'Federal Scheme' was taken from the Government of India Act 1935, but the concept of a 'Federation with a strong Centre' was borrowed from the Canadian Constitution. (Note: The word 'Federation' is nowhere used in the Indian Constitution).

mnemonics_and_tricks.trick_title: Ideals of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The ideals of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity in our Preamble are directly taken from the French Revolution (1789-1799).
The ideal of Justice (Social, Economic, and Political) in the Preamble is inspired by the Russian Revolution (1917).

exam_strategy_tips: In Assertion-Reasoning questions, perfectly align the Supreme Court cases: Berubari (1960 - Not a part), Kesavananda Bharati (1973 - Is a part), LIC of India (1995 - Integral part).
Focus heavily on the 'Borrowed Features' mapping; it is a highly recurring question in UPSC and State PCS examinations.
